Git and GitHub

Let’s start with the basics. Git is a version control system that allows you to track changes to your files and collaborate with others It is used to manage the history of your code and to merge changes from different branches. I can understand that as of now these terms like version control, branches, and merges are not familiar to you. But don’t worry, we will learn them in this tutorial.

Git and Github are different

Git is a version control system that is used to track changes to your files. It is a free and open-source software that is available for Windows, macOS, and Linux. Remember, GIT is a software and can be installed on your computer.

Github is a web-based hosting service for Git repositories. Github is an online platform that allows you to store and share your code with others. It is a popular platform for developers to collaborate on projects and to share code. It is not that Github is the only provider of Git repositories, but it is one of the most popular ones.

A little on version control systems

Version control systems are used to manage the history of your code. They allow you to track changes to your files and to collaborate with others. Version control systems are essential for software development. Consider version control as a checkpoint in game. You can move to any time in the game and you can always go back to the previous checkpoint. This is the same concept in software development. 

Before Git became mainstream, version control systems were used by developers to manage their code. They were called SCCS (Source Code Control System). SCCS was a proprietary software that was used to manage the history of code. It was expensive and not very user-friendly. Git was created to replace SCCS and to make version control more accessible and user-friendly. Some commong version control systems are Subversion (SVN), CVS, and Perforce.

Learning Path

In this tutorial, we will learn the basics of Git and Github. We will start with the basics and then move on to more advanced topics. We will also learn how to use Git and Github for collaboration and version control. By the end of this tutorial, you will have a good understanding of Git and Github and will be able to use them to manage your code effectively.

We will go in this jounney something like this:

  • Get the basics
  • Use it daily
  • Face the problems
  • Solve them
  • Learn more

We will focus more on Git first, once you understand git, moving towards Github will be easy.

Install Git

To install Git, you can use command line or you can visit official website and download the installer for your operating system. Git is available for Windows, macOS, and Linux and is available at https://git-scm.com/downloads.

Account on Github

Another step that you have to follow is to create an account on Github. I will later walk you through the process of linking your Github account with your Machine. You cannot push your code to Github without ssh-key setup. Password authentication is not recommended and these days it is not possible to use it. So, you need to setup ssh-key authentication. We will cover that in a later part of the tutorial.

Conclusion

In this part, we have learned the basics of Git and Github. We have also learned how to install Git and Github. We have also learned about the importance of version control systems and how they are used in software development.


Terminology

Git and people who use it talk in a different terminology. For example they don’t call it a folder, they call it a repository. They don’t call it alternative timeline, they call it branch. Although, I agree that alternative timeline is a better name for it. 😁

Check your git version

To check your git version, you can run the following command:

This command will display the version of git installed on your system. Git is a very stable software and don’t get any breaking changes in majority of the cases, at least in my experience.

Repository (FOLDER KA NAAM) 

A repository is a collection of files and directories that are stored together. It is a way to store and manage your code. A repository is like a folder on your computer, but it is more than just a folder. It can contain other files, folders, and even other repositories. You can think of a repository as a container that holds all your code.

There is a difference between a software on your system vs tracking a particular folder on your system. At any point you can run the following command to see the current state of your repository:

Not all folders are meant to be tracked by git. Here we can see that all green folders are projects are getting tracked by git but red ones are not.

Your config settings

Github has a lot of settings that you can change. You can change your username, email, and other settings. Whenever you checkpoint your changes, git will add some information about your such as your username and email to the commit. There is a git config file that stores all the settings that you have changed. You can make settings like what editor you would like to use etc. There are some global settings and some repository specific settings.

Let’s setup your email and username in this config file. I would recommend you to create an account on github and then use the email and username that you have created.

Now you can check your config settings:

This will show you all the settings that you have changed.



Creating a repository

Creating a repository is a process of creating a new folder on your system and initializing it as a git repository. It’s just regular folder to code your project, you are just asking git to track it. To create a repository, you can use the following command:

git status command will show you the current state of your repository. git init command will create a new folder on your system and initialize it as a git repository. This adds a hidden .git folder to your project.

Commit

commit is a way to save your changes to your repository. It is a way to record your changes and make them permanent. You can think of a commit as a snapshot of your code at a particular point in time. When you commit your changes, you are telling git to save them in a permanent way. This way, you can always go back to that point in time and see what you changed.

proper flow 

When you want to track a new folder, you first use init command to create a new repository. Then you can use add command to add the folder to the repository. After that you can use commit command to save the changes. Finally you can use push command to push the changes to github. Of course there is more to it but this is the basic flow.

Stage

Stage is a way to tell git to track a particular file or folder. You can use the following command to stage a file:

Here we are initializing the repository and adding a file to the repository. Then we can see that the file is now being tracked by git. Currently our files are in staging area, this means that we have not yet committed the changes but are ready to be committed.

Commit

Here we are committing the changes to the repository. We can see that the changes are now committed to the repository. The -m flag is used to add a message to the commit. This message is a short description of the changes that were made. You can use this message to remember what the changes were. Missing the -m flag will result in an action that opens your default settings editor, which is usually VIM. We will change this to vscode in the next section.

Logs

This command will show you the history of your repository. It will show you all the commits that were made to the repository. You can use the --oneline flag to show only the commit message. This will make the output more compact and easier to read. (important)

☕️ - Check git log docs

Atomic commits are a way to make sure that each commit is a self-contained unit of work. This means that if one commit fails, you can always go back to a previous commit and fix the issue. This is important for maintaining a clean and organized history in your repository.

Conclusion

In this section, we have learned about the basics of git and how to use it to track changes to your files and folders. We have also learned about the different commands that you can use to interact with your repository, such as init, add, commit, log, etc By the end of this section, you should have a good understanding of how to use git and how to use it effectively to manage your code.

Git behind the scenes

Git is a version control system that allows you to track changes to your files and folders. It is a powerful tool that can help you manage your code more effectively. In this section, we will explore the basics of how git works internally. almost ek database tpye system bnake rkhta h key value pair ki trh ; git ke internal architecture me object honge ; 


every commit has a unique id in the backend ; har hash nya pe dependent hota h 

Git Snapshots

A git snapshot is a point in time in the history of your code. It represents a specific version of your code, including all the files and folders that were present at that time. Each snapshot is identified by a unique hash code, which is a string of characters that represents the contents of the snapshot.

A snapshot is not an image, it’s just a representation of the code at a specific point in time. Snapshot is a loose term that is used when git stores information about the code in a locally stored key-value based database. Everything is stored as an object and each object is identified by a unique hash code.

3 Musketeers of Git

The three musketeers of git are:

  • Commit Object
  • Tree Object
  • Blob Object

Commit Object

Each commit in the project is stored in .git folder in the form of a commit object. A commit object contains the following information:

  • Tree Object
  • Parent Commit Object
  • Author
  • Committer
  • Commit Message

Tree Object

Tree Object is a container for all the files and folders in the project. It contains the following information:

  • File Mode
  • File Name
  • File Hash
  • Parent Tree Object

Everything is stored as key-value pairs in the tree object. The key is the file name and the value is the file hash.


q se quit 

Blob Object

Blob Object is present in the tree object and contains the actual file content. This is the place where the file content is stored.

These are detailed notes on Git basics, strictly following the flow, terminology, and examples provided in the sources.
1. Difference Between Git and GitHub
  • Git: It is an original software used for version control.
  • GitHub: It is an online service used to host the Git software.
  • Key Insight: You must not confuse the two; Git is the core software, while services like GitHub or GitLab are online tools that may change over time.
2. What is Git? (The Gaming Analogy)
  • Git is best understood through the example of video games.
  • In a game, you save your progress at different checkpoints (e.g., Stage 1, Stage 3, Stage 5).
  • If something goes wrong in your code, Git allows you to return to any previous checkpoint.
  • It is a Version Control System (VCS) that tracks changes in files.
  • Before Git, there were other tools like SCCS, SVN, CVS, and Perforce, but Git became mainstream because it is open-source and free.
3. Setup and Environment
  • Terminal: For Windows users, Git Bash is recommended because it supports commands like ls. Mac users can use Warp or the simple terminal.
  • Code Editor: VS Code is preferred.
  • Visualization: The "Git Graph" extension helps visualize the trajectory of Git branches.
  • Documentation: Notes and commands can be referenced at docs.chaicode.com.
4. Configuration (Global Settings)
  • Check Version: Use git --version to see your current version.
  • Identity: When tracking files, Git saves your information so it can be pushed online later.
    • Set Email: git config --global user.email "your@email.com".
    • Set Name: git config --global user.name "Your Name".
    • View Settings: git config --list.
  • Rule: Always use double quotes ("") for values to avoid issues with spaces or special characters.
5. Repositories (The "Repo")
  • In the software industry, a folder or directory is called a "Repo".
  • Check Status: Before starting, always run git status to see if a folder is already a Git repository.
  • Initialization: To start tracking a folder, use git init.
    • This creates a hidden folder named .git.
    • The .git folder contains the internal database (Objects, Refs, Head, Config) that manages your checkpoints.
6. The Core Workflow: Write → Add → Commit
The entire Git journey revolves around this flow:
  1. Working Directory: This is where you write your code (e.g., creating file1.txt).
  2. Staging Area: Use git add <file_name> or git add . to move changes here.
    • Analogy: Everyone is on the "stage," but the performance (checkpoint) hasn't started yet.
  3. Repository (Local): Use git commit -m "message" to save changes to the local repo.
    • This creates a permanent checkpoint on your system.
  4. Remote: Finally, use git push to send the code to GitHub.
7. Commit Guidelines and Logs
  • Atomic Commits: Git recommends committing a "unit of work" (e.g., just the footer) rather than thousands of files at once. This makes it easier to go back if needed.
  • Message Tone: Use Present Tense and Imperative tone (giving an order to the code base), such as "Add footer to code base" instead of "Added footer".
  • Viewing History:
    • git log: Shows full history (Commit ID, Author, Date, Message).
    • git log --oneline: Shows a condensed, one-line version of the history.
8. Specialized Files: .gitignore and .gitkeep
  • .gitignore: Used to list files you do not want to track (e.g., .env files with secrets, node_modules, or large images).
  • .gitkeep: Since Git does not track empty folders, placing a blank file named .gitkeep inside a folder forces Git to track that directory.
9. Branching Basics
  • Definition: A branch is an alternative timeline (like in Spider-Man or Dr. Strange movies).
  • Head: A pointer that indicates which branch you are currently on.
  • Commands:
    • git branch: Lists available branches.
    • git branch <name>: Creates a new branch (e.g., git branch bug-fix).
    • git switch <name>: Moves you to that branch.
    • git switch -c <name>: Creates a new branch and switches to it simultaneously.
  • Merging: To bring work from a side branch (like bug-fix) into the main branch, use git merge <branch_name> while on the main branch.


Segment 3: Terminology, Configuration, and Initialization
1. Terminology: What is a "Repo"?
  • In the software industry, people like to give things their own names.
  • Some call it a "Folder," some call it a "Directory," but in Git, we call it a "Repo" (short for Repository).
  • Internally they are the same thing, but "Repo" is the professional term used to discuss the project environment.
2. Checking the Git Version
  • The first command to run is git --version.
  • Stability of Git: Git is an extremely stable software. Unlike other tools, it rarely has "breaking changes."
  • Whether you use a version from today or from three to five years ago, 99.99% of the features and commands will remain the same.
3. Setting Your Identity (Git Config)
  • When you track files, Git saves your information so it knows who made the changes.
  • This is important so that when you push code to GitHub or GitLab, your identity is saved with the code.
  • Two Levels of Config:
    1. Global File: Settings that apply to every repository on your system.
    2. Repository Level: Specific settings for just one project.
  • Essential Commands:
    • Set Global Email: git config --global user.email "your@email.com"
    • Set Global Name: git config --global user.name "Your Name"
    • The Quote Rule: Always put your email and name in double quotes ("") to avoid issues with spaces or special characters.
    • View all settings: git config --list
4. Creating a Repository (git init)
  • The Investigative Step: Before creating a repo, always run git status.
  • If you run git status in a normal folder, it will show an error: "not a git repository."
  • Initialization: To turn a folder into a repo, use the command git init.
  • Investigating the Output: When you run git init, Git might give you a message about the "initial branch" (usually named Master or Main). It also tells you how to rename the branch if you wish.
5. The Hidden .git Folder
  • Running git init creates a hidden folder named .git inside your project.
  • What's Inside: This folder is roughly 80-90% like a database. It stores all your progress and checkpoints.
  • If you look inside .git (using ls -a or ls -la in the terminal), you will see several files and folders:
    • HEAD: Points to the current branch.
    • config: Stores repository-specific settings.
    • description: Used by the Gitweb program.
    • hooks: Scripts that run at certain points (like before a commit).
    • info, objects, refs: The internal structure for storing data and references.
  • Caution: Never manually override or delete the .git folder unless you want to lose all your checkpoints and progress.
6. The "Green" vs. "Red" Concept
  • In this course’s visualization, a "Green" folder is one being tracked by Git (it has a .git folder).
  • A "Red" folder is a normal directory that is not being tracked by Git.
  • You don't have to track every folder on your computer; each project runs at its own speed and has its own tracking mechanism.

Segment 4: The Core Workflow and Commit Philosophy
1. The Three-Step Journey (Write → Add → Commit)
  • The entire journey of Git is based on a simple flow: Write, Add, and Commit.
  • The Workflow:
    1. Write: You start in the Working Directory (your folder). This is where you write your code or create files.
    2. Add: You run the git add command to move your work to the Staging Area.
    3. Commit: You run the git commit command to save your work in the Repo (the local repository).
  • Final Step: Once saved in the local repo, you can use the push command to send it to GitHub. For now, the focus is only on the local Repo.
2. Understanding the Staging Area (The Analogy)
  • Think of the Staging Area as a stage for a performance.
  • When you "Add" files, you are bringing everyone onto the stage.
  • They are ready and standing there, but the performance has not started yet. The performance only starts when you Commit.
3. Practical Demonstration: Creating and Adding Files
  • Step 1 (Write): Create a file (e.g., file1.txt) and add some text.
  • Step 2 (Add): You have two main ways to use the add command:
    • Specific: git add file1.txt — This is the recommended way because you manually choose what to stage.
    • All at once: git add . — The dot (.) means "add everything." People use this when they have worked on many files (e.g., 15-20 files) and want to stage them all together.
4. Checking Status and Committing
  • Status: After adding, git status will show "Changes to be committed" in green. It tells you that new files are on the stage but not yet committed.
  • The Commit: Use the command git commit -m "your message".
  • The Importance of -m: You must use the -m flag to provide a message. Without it, Git will not save the checkpoint easily.
  • Success: Once committed, Git confirms that the files are saved in the Repo. This is your permanent checkpoint.
5. Viewing History (Logs)
  • To see what you have done so far, use the Logs.
  • git log: Shows a very large ID (SHA ID), the Author, the Date, and the Message.
  • git log --oneline: Because the full log is very long, developers use this "flag" to see a condensed, one-line version of the history.
6. Philosophy: Atomic Commits
  • Git does not recommend working on 1,000 files or 10,000 features and then committing them all at once.
  • Instead, you should do "Atomic Commits".
  • Definition: A commit should represent a single "Unit of Work".
  • Example: If you are building a website footer, as soon as that specific unit (the footer) is done, you should commit it. This makes it much easier to go back to a specific point if something breaks.
7. Philosophy: The Tone of Commit Messages
  • While personal choice exists, the professional industry and Git recommend a specific tone: Present Tense and Imperative.
  • The Rule: You should "Give an order to the code base".
  • Examples:
    • Use: "Add footer to code base".
    • Avoid: "Added footer" (Past tense).

Segment 5: Specialized Files and Git Internals
1. The Git Ignore File (.gitignore)
  • In every project folder, there are often important but sensitive files that you do not want to track or push to GitHub.
  • Example: A .env file containing an "API Secret" or "Payment Gateway Code".
  • The Problem: If you leave these files as they are, git status will continuously "complain" to you that these files are untracked.
  • The Solution: Create a special file named .gitignore at the root of your project.
  • Inside this file, simply list the names of the files or folders you want to ignore (e.g., .env or node_modules).
  • Once added to .gitignore, Git will stop tracking them and they will "disappear" from your tracking list.
2. The Git Keep Trick (.gitkeep)
  • A specific characteristic of Git is that it does not track empty folders.
  • Example: If you create a folder for "Images" or "Logs" but haven't put anything in them yet, git status will not show them.
  • The Professional Trick: Since you want the folder structure to remain, place a blank file named .gitkeep inside the empty folder.
  • This forces Git to recognize and track the folder even if it has no actual project files yet.
  • agar aapko koi empty folder ko bhi dhyan me krahan jo ki git ingote krta h toh aap use kroge gitkeep har folder me 
3. Git Internals: "Behind the Scenes"
  • This section is designed to take you "out of the box" and away from straightforward Git knowledge to improve your engineering perspective.
  • SHA ID: Behind the scenes, every single commit is assigned a very large, unique identification number called a SHA ID.
  • Git as a Database: Internally, Git functions almost like a database system. It stores information in key-value pairs using hash tables.
  • Snapshots: Git works by taking "Snapshots" (like a photo) of how your code looks at a specific point in time. It doesn't just store the changes; it manages Blob objects which are the files in their exact format.
4. The "Three Musketeers" of Git The creator uses the term "Three Musketeers" to describe the three major pillars of Git's internal storage:
  1. Commit Object: This is the top layer. It stores the reference to the Tree object, the parent commit (if it exists), author/committer info (name, email), and the commit message.
  2. Tree Object: This sits in the middle. It stores the file mode, file name, and the file's hash. It acts as a reference point to reach the actual files.
  3. Blob Object: This is the actual code or file content itself.
  4. The Internal Flow: Commit Object → Tree Object → Blob Object.
5. Engineering Perspective
  • You will likely never be asked about these internals in a basic interview, nor will you manually manipulate them daily.
  • However, knowing that Git manages a full structure of trees, refs, and blobs—rather than just "running four commands"—gives you a true engineering perspective.

Segment 6: Porcelain vs. Plumbing and the Manual Git Process
1. The Distinction: Porcelain vs. Plumbing
  • Git categorizes its commands into two types based on how they interact with the system.
  • Porcelain Commands: These are the "fancy" commands you use daily (e.g., git add, git commit).
    • They provide a "fancy layer" or interface so you don't have to worry about internal details.
    • upr upr se krna ;
  • Plumbing (or Gardening) Commands: These are the low-level, manual commands that Git runs behind the scenes.
    • Using these is like doing everything manually rather than using an automated interface.
    • While developers use Porcelain commands 99% of the time, the Plumbing commands do the actual heavy lifting.
2. Investigative Demo: Manual Commit (The "Gardening" Way) The source demonstrates how to manually create a commit without using git add or git commit to show what happens internally.
  • Setup: A new folder (named "Four") is initialized with git init.
  • Step 1: Creating a File: A file named test.txt is created.
  • Step 2: Generating a Hash (hash-object): Instead of git add, the command git hash-object is used to manually generate a unique SHA-1 hash for the file.
  • Step 3: Updating the Index (update-index): To move the file to the "staged" version manually, the command git update-index --add --cacheinfo is used.
    • This requires providing file permissions, the SHA-1 hash generated in the previous step, and the filename.
  • Step 4: Writing the Tree (write-tree): After indexing, a Tree Object must be created manually using git write-tree. This captures the structure of the files.
  • Step 5: Creating the Commit (commit-tree): A Commit Object is created using git commit-tree.
    • This links the Tree Object to a message (e.g., "Initial commit").
    • If previous commits existed, you would also have to manually manage the "Parent" and "Head" references.
  • Step 6: Updating the Reference (update-ref): Finally, the command git update-ref refs/heads/master is used to point the Master branch to the new commit hash.
3. The Engineering Perspective
  • Not for Daily Use: The source explicitly states that no one is recommended to follow this manual process for daily work, and it is rarely asked in basic interviews.
  • The Value: Knowing these internals provides an "Engineering Perspective".
  • It shows that Git is not just about "running four commands" but is actually managing a complex structure of Trees, Refs, and Blobs in an internal database.
  • Understanding this "uncomfortable" level of detail makes the standard add and commit commands feel much easier and more logical.
4. Summary of Internal Structure
  • As seen in the hidden .git folder during this manual process:
    • Objects: Store the actual data (Blobs) and structures (Trees).
    • Refs/Heads: Store where the branches (like Master) are pointing.
    • HEAD: A file that tracks which branch you are currently on.

Segment 7: Git Branches and Alternative Timelines

1. Importance of Branches
  • Branches are often a developer's favorite topic because they are the tool that allows a team to work together seamlessly.
  • They allow you to work on multiple features at the same time without them interfering with each other.
  • Example: If you are building documentation for both "Django" and "Git," you can keep a Main branch that is published and create separate branches for "Django" and "Git." When one is finished, you merge it into the Main branch while continuing work on the other in its own alternative timeline.


2. The Concept: Alternative Timelines
  • The easiest way to understand a branch is as an "Alternative Timeline."
  • Pop Culture Analogy: For those who watch movies like Spider-Man or Doctor Strange’s Multiverse, this concept is easy. You can have different versions of events happening simultaneously in different ecosystems.
  • Parallel Work: In Git, a branch (like a Blue line or Green line) runs separately from the Main (Orange) line. Work done in one does not bother the other until you intentionally merge them.
3. The "Head" Pointer
  • Definition: "Head" is a pointer that indicates which branch you are currently on.
  • The Tape Recorder Analogy: This concept comes from old music systems or tape recorders. In those systems, there was a physical "head" placed on the tape. Wherever the head was placed, the music would start playing from that point.
  • In Git: Wherever the "Head" is pointing, that is where Git starts writing and saving your code.
  • git branch krne se bta chl jaata h 

4. Basic Branch Commands
  • git branch: Running this command alone shows you a list of your branches and highlights the one you are currently on (usually marked with a star).
  • git branch <name>: This command creates a new branch with the name you provide (e.g., git branch bug-fix).
    • Note: Creating a branch does not automatically move you into it. Your "Head" will still point to the original branch until you switch.
    • isse toh git branch branch ka name likhdoge toh nya branch bn jaayega ; 
5. Switching Branches
  • git switch <name>: This moves your "Head" to the specified branch (e.g., git switch bug-fix).
  • Verification: After switching, you can check the hidden .git folder’s "HEAD" file; it will now show the reference to your new branch.
6. Practical Example: The Disappearing File
agar aap ek branch me ek file aage ho or commit krdi ab aap branch switch kroge toh woh wali file apko main branch me nhi dikhegi 

  • If you switch to a bug-fix branch and create a new file (e.g., fix.txt) and commit it, that file exists in that alternative timeline.
  • When you switch back to the Master branch (git switch master), the fix.txt file will disappear from your folder.
  • Why? Because you have moved back to a timeline where that file was never created. This allows you to work on features without messing up your main code.
7. Advanced Switching and Checkout
  • git switch -c <name>: This is a combined command. It creates a new branch and switches to it at the same time.
  • acha h yr yeh toh ; 
  • git checkout <name>: You will often see developers using "checkout" instead of "switch." It is an older, very common command used to move between branches (e.g., git checkout orange-mode).
    • Note: If you try to checkout a branch that doesn't exist, Git will give an error.


Segment 8: Merging and Conflict Resolution

1. Bringing the Work Together
  • The work done in an "Alternative Timeline" (branch) shouldn't stay there forever; eventually, it must be brought back into the main code.
  • Visualizing the Flow: Using "Git Graph" is helpful here to see how a side branch (like a blue line) deviates from the main branch (orange line) and eventually needs to be mixed back in.
  • download it in vs code 

  • ise smjh arha h master or new-branch ek jgh pe h or bug-fix wali ek aage h 
2. Fast-Forward Merge
  • The Scenario: This occurs when you create a branch, perform some work (like a bug fix), but the main branch has not changed at all since you branched off.
  • The Procedure:
    1. Switch to the branch that needs to receive the work (e.g., git switch master).
    2. Run the merge command: git merge bug-fix.
  • The Result: Because the main branch was static, Git simply "fast-forwards" the pointer to the latest work. It is a very clean and straightforward process.

3. Non-Fast-Forward Merge (The Manual Merge)
  • The Scenario: This happens when work has progressed on both branches simultaneously. For example, while you were fixing a bug on one branch, someone else added a marketing message to the master branch. mtlb dono me kuch na kuch kaam horha h ab kese merge hoga kon prioritise krega 
  • The Procedure: When you run git merge bug-fix on the master branch, Git realizes the timelines have diverged.

4. Handling Merge Conflicts
  • What is a Conflict? A conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically decide which code to keep—specifically when the exact same line in the same file has been modified differently in both branches.
  • The "2024 vs. 2025" Example:
    • In the Master branch, you added a note: "2024 is coming".
    • In the Bug-fix branch, in the same file, you added: "2025 and footer note added".
    • When you attempt to merge, Git "complains" and stops because it doesn't know which year is correct.
5. Resolving the Conflict
  • The Visual Markers: Inside the conflicting file, Git adds special symbols:
    • <<<<<<< HEAD: Shows what is in your current branch.
    • =======: The divider between the two versions.
    • >>>>>>> bug-fix: Shows what is coming from the other branch.

  • The Resolution Process: You must manually choose one of the options in VS Code: Accept Current Change, Accept Incoming Change, or Accept Both.

6. Aborting a Merge
  • If the conflict looks too complicated or "messy" and you aren't ready to fix it, you can use the command git merge --abort. This cancels the merge and returns everything to exactly how it was before you started.

segment 9: Git Diff, Stashing, and Tags

1. Introduction to the Segment
  • This section moves away from the complexity of branching into three easier but essential tools: Git Diff, Stashing, and Tags.
  • The creator notes that while branching can be difficult for beginners, these topics are more straightforward.
  • The Setup: To demonstrate, the creator ensures the "master" branch is clean using git status and then adds a new line of text ("Another marketing section") to file1.txt.
2. Git Diff: The Informational Tool
  • Definition: git diff is an informing command. Much like git log, it does not change the state of your project; it simply provides information.
  • The Investigative Step: Running git diff by itself often produces no output if changes are already staged. To see changes that have been added to the staging area, you must use git diff --staged.
  • Reading the Output (The Marking System):
    • You will see lines like --- a/file1.txt and +++ b/file1.txt.
    • The Clarification: People often assume --- means deleted and +++ means added. The creator clarifies that these are just markers for "Version A" and "Version B" of the same file.
    • Internally, Git treats these as two different objects (unique IDs) and compares them.
    • The + sign next to a specific line of text indicates that this text is the difference found in the "Version B" (the newer version).
3. Comparing Commits
  • You can use git diff to compare any two points in time.
  • The Syntax: The most common professional way to compare two commits is using the "dot-dot" (..) syntax: git diff <commit_id_1>..<commit_id_2>.
  • This allows you to see exactly what changed between two specific checkpoints in your history.
4. Git Stash: The Temporary Storage
  • The Scenario: Suppose you are working on a feature in the "master" branch. Suddenly, you need to switch to a "bug-fix" branch to help a teammate.
  • The Problem: If you try to switch branches with uncommitted changes, Git will "complain" and stop you because your work-in-progress would be lost.
  • The Solution: If you aren't ready to commit (because the work is incomplete), you use git stash.
  • How it Works:
    • git stash takes your current changes and puts them in a temporary location (like a stack memory).
    • This "cleans" your working directory, allowing you to switch branches freely.
  • Managing Stashes:
    • git stash list: Shows a list of all your saved stashes (e.g., stash@{0}, stash@{1}).
    • git stash apply: Brings the changes back from the stash to your current branch.
    • git stash pop: This is a very common command. it applies the changes and simultaneously deletes (drops) them from the stash list.
5. Git Tags: The "Sticky Note"
  • Definition: Think of a Tag as a sticky note that you attach to a specific commit to make it stand out.
  • Usage: Tags are not used for every commit. They are usually reserved for Major Releases.
  • Examples: You might tag a commit as v1.0, Beta-Release, or Canary-Version.
  • Commands:
    • git tag <name>: Adds a basic tag to your current commit.
    • git tag -a <name> -m "message": Creates an Annotated Tag, which allows you to add a descriptive note (like a release message).
    • git tag: Lists all tags in the repository.
  • Professional Tip: Usually, individual developers don't create tags for everything. This is typically handled by Product Managers or Release Managers when a specific version of the software is ready for the public.



Segment 10: Git Rebase and Git Reflog
1. The "Scary" Reputation of Git Rebase
  • Git Rebase is often considered the most intimidating command in Git.
  • The Warning: Many developers are told to avoid Rebase because it rewrites history. If you do not understand how it works, you can "mess up" the entire codebase.
  • The Reality: While you should remain cautious, it is an essential tool for creating a clean commit history.
2. What is Rebase? (The Concept)
  • Definition: Rebase is a tool used to change the base of a branch.
  • How it Works: It effectively moves a branch to a new starting point (usually a different commit) by "replaying" your original commits on top of a new base.
  • The Diagram Analogy:
    • Imagine you branch off from Master to work on a feature.
    • While you are working, someone else pushes new code to Master.
    • Normally, you would "Merge" Master into your branch, creating an extra, unnecessary "Merge Commit".
    • Rebase instead takes your entire branch and shifts its starting point from the old Master commit to the latest Master commit.
3. Practical Benefits of Rebase
  • Cleaner History: Unlike merging, which creates "pollution" in the logs with multiple "Merge branch..." messages, Rebase results in a linear, clean timeline.
  • No Extra Commits: Rebase does not create an additional commit just to link two branches; it simply re-aligns the base.
  • Professional Standard: Many large organizations require developers to Rebase before pushing code to keep the project history easy to read.
4. Git Reflog: The Ultimate History Tool
  • Definition: git reflog is a command that shows the complete history of your commits and movements in the repository over time.
  • Difference from Log: While git log shows the history of the branch, git reflog shows everywhere the "Head" has moved—even if you deleted a branch or made a mistake.
  • The Benefit: It allows you to see exactly where you were at any point (e.g., 15 minutes ago or 3 commits ago).
5. Recovering Lost Work using Reflog and Reset
  • Reflog is primarily used to recover lost commits or changes.
  • The Process:
    1. Run git reflog to find the unique SHA-1 hash of the point where your code was still safe.
    2. Use the command git reset --hard <commit_id> to return your entire codebase to that exact state.
  • Caution: git reset --hard should be used very carefully because once you jump to that commit, the changes you left behind are difficult to recover.
  • The Head Shortcut: You can also use HEAD@{1} or HEAD@{2} to go back one or two steps, but the source recommends using specific commit IDs from the log to be 100% precise.
6. Summary of Engineering Perspective
  • By understanding these internals (Rebase, Reflog, and Resets), you gain a true engineering perspective.
  • You are no longer just a person who "runs four commands"; you are someone who can manage complex structures, recover from errors, and maintain a professional codebase

Segment 11: GitHub, SSH Keys, and Pushing Code
1. What is GitHub?
  • GitHub is a web-based Git repository service.
  • Just as you create a repository on your local system, you can create a clone of that repository online. This acts as an online backup.
  • You can choose to keep your repository Public or Private.
  • The Industry Context: While GitHub is the most mainstream and popular platform today, it is not the only one. Alternatives include GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure Repo, and Gitea.
  • Corporate Security: High-level or security-conscious companies often use the Enterprise Edition. In this case, the Git software is used, but the code is stored on the company’s own servers rather than public GitHub servers.
2. Identity and Configuration
  • Account Setup: You must create an account on GitHub using your email and a unique username.
  • Local Sync: Ensure your local system's global configuration (email and username) matches your GitHub details using the git config --list command.
3. SSH Keys: The Mandatory Connection
  • For the last few years, GitHub has not allowed communication via standard ID and password through the command line.
  • The Solution: You must use SSH Keys.
  • How it Works: You generate a "Key" on your local system and provide a copy of that key (the signature) to GitHub. When you send a request from your system, GitHub recognizes the verified signature and allows the connection.
  • Generating the Key:
    • Use the command ssh-keygen -t <algorithm_type> -C "your_email@example.com".
    • This generates a Public/Private key pair.
    • You may be asked for a "Passphrase" (a password for your key). You can leave it empty if you don't want to enter it every time you commit, or set one for extra security.
  • Adding to GitHub: You must find the generated .pub file, copy its text content, and paste it into the "SSH and GPG keys" section of your GitHub account settings.
4. Pushing Local Code to GitHub
  • Step 1: Create an Online Repo: On GitHub, click "New Repository." Give it a name (e.g., git-hindi) and click "Create Repository".
  • Step 2: Connecting Local to Remote:
    • Use the command: git remote add origin <your_github_url>.
    • Terminology: "Origin" is simply the most common name for your remote connection. You could technically name it anything (like "Superman"), but "Origin" is the professional standard.
    • Verification: Run git remote -v to see your verified fetch and push links.
  • Step 3: The First Push:
    • Command: git push -u origin main.
    • The -u Flag (Upstream): This sets a permanent link (upstream) between your local branch and the remote branch. Once this is set, you can simply type git push in the future, and Git will automatically know where to send the code.
5. The README File
  • Git repositories usually expect a file named readme.md in the root folder.
  • Formatting: This is a Markdown file. It is used to provide installation instructions or documentation for anyone viewing your repository online.
  • Once you create and commit a readme.md locally, GitHub will automatically display its content on your repository's main page.

Segment 12: Open Source Contribution and Ethics
1. The Philosophy and Caution of Open Source
  • Open source is very popular today, but it must be approached with extreme caution.
  • The Salary Misconception: Some people believe that doing open source will automatically land them a 5-crore or 10-crore package. The creator notes this is often far from reality.
  • The Responsibility of Scale: Because of the high population in countries like India, even a small mistake by many people creates a massive global impact. If 50,000 people do something wrong, it is a huge problem for international maintainers.
  • Profile vs. Reputation: Trying to "hack" your profile by making low-quality contributions for a job will actually lower your reputation and the reputation of your country.
2. The "Talk First" Rule
  • This is the most important step in open source.
  • The Procedure: Before writing any code, you must talk to the community first. Ask: "What can I contribute?", "Is there a bug I can fix?", or "Is there an issue I should handle?".
  • Avoid Spam: The community often dislikes "Readme fixes" or "grammar fixes" if they are done just to increase contribution counts. As a programmer, you should focus on adding functional value (features/bugs) rather than just being a content writer.
3. The Professional Mindset
  • Value Addition: Always ask if you are actually adding value to the project.
  • No Guarantees: There is no guarantee that you will get a T-shirt, money, or a job. Open source is a proof that you can understand a heavy, existing codebase and contribute back to the community.
4. The Technical Workflow of Open Source
  • Step 1: Communication. Join the project's Discord or Slack and talk to the maintainers.
  • Step 2: Forking. Click the "Fork" button on GitHub to create a copy of the repository under your own account. This shows you are working on a copy, not the original.
  • Step 3: Cloning. Bring your forked version to your local system using git clone.
  • Step 4: Feature Development. Spend real time (weeks or months) developing the feature. It is not a "joke" or a "one-day" task.
  • Step 5: Commit and Push. Use the standard add, commit, and push commands to save your work to your forked repository.
  • Step 6: Pull Request (PR). Once your work is ready, click "Contribute" and then "Open Pull Request" on GitHub.
    • The PR Rule: You must provide full details and a nice description in Markdown explaining exactly what you changed and why it helps.
5. Practicing Safely
  • The creator has a specific repository named "Open Source Contribution" on his profile (hiteshchoudhary) where people can practice without bothering serious maintainers.
  • The Warning: Do not "play" with big repositories like NumPy or Pandas because you will add an unnecessary workload to the maintainers who are already working hard.
